[batch narration moved out of reading 2026-09-02] CyrusOne is a large scale data center provider headquartered in Dallas, Texas. In 2016 CyrusOne purchased the Chicago Mercantile Exchanges original Aurora, Illinois data center from CME Group for roughly 130 million dollars, with CME Group continuing to operate its Globex matching engine on site under a 15 year lease. In November 2021, KKR and Global Infrastructure Partners agreed to acquire CyrusOne in an approximately 15 billion dollar deal, taking the company private, and that acquisition closed in 2022. CyrusOne has operated as a privately held company since, a company level ownership fact this registry had not previously recorded with a citable source. This specific row, Norwalk, corresponds to this operators own NYM5 site code. The operators own current data center locations page, fetched fresh this session, confirms this facility as Connecticuts largest data center located in Norwalk, CT, though it does not itself publish a street address. Two independent aggregator listings, datacenterHawk and datacentermap, both fetched fresh this session, agree on 6 Norden Place as the street address. One of the two, datacenterHawk, labels the surrounding city as Stamford rather than Norwalk, which this session resolved in favor of the operators own explicit Norwalk, CT city confirmation and datacentermaps independent Norwalk listing.

reading.body:
CyrusOne Norwalk is Connecticut's largest published data center with 4 MW of critical IT load capacity. At a typical AI training density of 40 kW per rack, this translates roughly to 100 racks. The facility occupies 168,000 square feet at 6 Norden Place in Norwalk, placing it in the dense Northeast corridor where power constraints are acute.

This campus represents half of Connecticut's total published data center capacity of 8 MW across two facilities. The state has five mapped data centers on record, but most publish no specifications, meaning the true scope of Connecticut's installed base and its grid exposure remain unmeasured. Norwalk's published 4 MW is the largest single figure the state's operators have disclosed.

The facility's capacity is modest relative to leading AI infrastructure campuses elsewhere, which measure in hundreds of megawatts. Connecticut's grid already carries the burden of dense urban and industrial load. A 4 MW facility in this context claims power density that is significant at the state scale, even though it represents a fraction of what large-scale AI training now requires, and the building's actual current utilization and tenant mix are not published.
